name: One-Way Switch
tagline: The simplest control there is: it makes or breaks a single conductor — and that conductor has to be the live one.
terminals: COM — common, the conductor arriving from the supply
L1 — switched live out to the lamp
Earth — plate earth terminal on metal faceplates
parts: Faceplate — the visible cover screwed to the back box
Rocker (or dolly) — the moving contact you press
Two fixing screws — top and bottom, into the back box lugs
Snap-action mechanism — springs the contacts open or closed in milliseconds
Rear terminals — cage clamps or screw terminals for the conductors
safety: A switch must interrupt live, never neutral. Wire it on neutral and the lampholder stays live with the light off — the classic reason a “dead” fitting still bites. Isolate and prove dead before you touch anything.

points.label: Faceplate
points.detail: The moulded cover that hides the mechanism and the back box. Switches are sold by gang (how many rockers) and by way (how many positions each rocker connects) — a one-gang one-way switch is the plain light switch.

points.label: Rocker
points.detail: Press the top, press the bottom: one movement closes the contacts, the next opens them. Inside is a spring that snaps the contacts across quickly, which is what keeps arcing (and pitting of the contacts) to a minimum.

points.label: Top fixing screw
points.detail: One of the two screws into the back box lugs. They only hold the plate on — they are not an earth path, so a metal faceplate still needs its earth flylead wired to the back box.

points.label: Bottom fixing screw
points.detail: The second fixing screw. Overtightening cracks the plate and can distort the back box enough to stop the rocker moving freely; just snug is right.

points.label: Rear terminals
points.detail: Two conductor terminals plus an earth: live in, switched live out. Brown sleeving on the switched live is not decoration — on a two-plate wiring system that conductor is live when the light is on and switched when it is off, so it must never be mistaken for a neutral.

points.label: Marking / rating
points.detail: The rating (commonly 10 A or 20 A) is the current the switch will carry continuously. It must equal or exceed the circuit protective device rating, and fluorescent or LED loads with a big inrush may call for a higher-rated switch.
